name: Goa
description: Goa is India's smallest state, defined by its Portuguese colonial heritage, palm-fringed beaches, and a laid-back coastal culture unlike anywhere else in the country. It suits beach lovers, party-goers, history buffs, and food tourists equally well, though peak-season crowds (November–February) can make beaches feel overcrowded and accommodation expensive. The monsoon (June–September) closes many shacks and water sports but brings lush greenery and significantly cheaper prices.
nearest_airport: Goa International Airport (Dabolim) / Manohar International Airport (Mopa)

attractions.name: Basilica of Bom Jesus
attractions.description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site housing the mortal remains of St. Francis Xavier, this 16th-century Baroque church is one of the finest examples of Portuguese colonial architecture in Asia. The interior is ornate but compact; the silver casket containing the saint's body is the main draw.

attractions.name: Sé Cathedral
attractions.description: One of the largest churches in Asia, the Sé Cathedral stands in Old Goa beside the Basilica and is also a UNESCO listed monument. The Golden Bell in its single surviving tower is reputedly the largest bell in Asia, and the interior retains several ornate carved altars.

attractions.name: Fort Aguada
attractions.description: A well-preserved 17th-century Portuguese fort at the mouth of the Mandovi river, offering sweeping views of the Arabian Sea and the Candolim coastline. The lower fort, lighthouse, and ramparts are freely accessible, though the upper section is occupied by a prison and is closed to visitors.

attractions.name: Palolem Beach
attractions.description: A crescent-shaped bay in South Goa widely considered the most scenic beach in the state, with calm waters suitable for swimming and a relaxed backpacker village behind the sand. It gets busy from December onwards but retains a quieter character than the North Goa party beaches.

attractions.name: Anjuna Flea Market
attractions.description: A Wednesday market that has operated since the 1970s hippie era, selling everything from Rajasthani textiles and silver jewellery to spices and electronics. Bargaining is expected and prices are not especially cheap, but the atmosphere is social and the crowd mix of tourists and local traders is distinctive.

attractions.name: Dudhsagar Falls
attractions.description: One of India's tallest waterfalls at roughly 310 metres, Dudhsagar cascades through dense Western Ghats forest on the Goa–Karnataka border. Access requires a bumpy jeep ride through Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary and is best visited in post-monsoon months (October–December) when the flow is strongest.

attractions.name: Chapora Fort
attractions.description: A ruined 17th-century fort above the Chapora river mouth, best known for its panoramic view over Vagator and the Arabian Sea. The fort itself is mostly rubble, but the viewpoint is genuinely spectacular and less crowded than Aguada; the short uphill walk is manageable but not paved.

attractions.name: Fontainhas Latin Quarter
attractions.description: Panaji's oldest neighbourhood, a maze of narrow lanes lined with ochre and terracotta Portuguese-era houses, a small chapel, and artisan workshops. It is genuinely walkable, free to explore, and offers the most authentic slice of Goa's Luso-Indian townscape without the beach-resort gloss.

attractions.name: Butterfly Beach
attractions.description: A tiny, isolated crescent of sand north of Palolem accessible only by boat or a difficult forest trail, largely unknown to mass tourism. It is genuinely quiet outside peak season and the boat ride from Palolem through the backwaters offers good dolphin-spotting chances.

attractions.name: Cabo de Rama Fort
attractions.description: A largely forgotten Portuguese fort on a dramatic headland between South Goa's Cola and Agonda beaches, offering cliff-top views that rival Chapora but attract a fraction of the visitors. The fort is in a state of ruin but the drive through cashew and coconut groves to reach it is pleasant in itself.
